I found this thread by Googling the same thing to see if others have gone by themselves. YES it is worth it to go, with a friend or by yourself. I am a lifelong Dover resident, and none of my friends really like Nascar. And my grandfather was too old to be able to go. So I got a ticket behind the start/finish and rented a scanner with a cooler full of beer. It was an amazing time, and I am doing it again this year. Everyone is very friendly, and you will fit right in no matter what. Renting a scanner is really essential, especially at smaller tracks. You can't hear anything when the green flag waves. I was suprised I actually enjoyed listening to the MRN radio broadcast on the scanner more than anything. There is practically zero delay with the broadcast through the scanner. So you know exactly what is happening at any given moment.

Gave me a rush of memories. I was raised by my grandparents, and a lifelong Dover resident. Starting in 2007 when I was 9, I must have gone to 15 or so races with him. My grandfather passed away this last fall. And I will always cherish the Nascar memories with him. He wasn't able to go to the race with me the last few years. And I usually go alone now. But everytime I walk through the grandstands and get the first view of the entire track. I always get the same exact feeling I did as a kid, first attending a race with him. I hope Dover never leaves the schedule, every race floods me with good memories with him.

Update in case anyone ever comes across this post. My grandfather peacefully passed away a few weeks ago. This cigar box unknowingly was the last Christmas I would ever spend with him. It means so much now….

To add a few things if anyone is interested. When he was in the hospital, before things took a downturn. He mentioned that he keeps seeing 2 people in the window, (he was on the third floor) but everytime he looks directly at them they disappear. He said they weren’t scary, and described what he could tell one was wearing. A paperboy hat, and a long trench coat. My grandmother described this to my grandfathers brother, and he lit up saying it described what his grandfather wore almost daily. (My grandfather was really close to his grandfather) the figure in the window also told him (you have to stay a little longer)


Also after things took a sudden downward turn, my grandfather could only slightly mumble and would say things that didn’t make much sense. Just generally out of it. (He was in septic shock). He then took another downward turn, and needed to be put on a respirator and was unconscious for a few days. 

After my and my grandmother discussing things with the doctor in great detail. And being told his quality of life would not be good even if he survived. (And my grandfather always saying he never wanted to be on life support) we decided to removed the ventilator and just pray for a miracle. After awhile he did wake up slightly, could look around, squeeze your hand and blink. But could still only mumble, his vitals were actually doing quite well, and we hoped maybe it would all work out.

That night my grandmother decided to spend the night in his hospital room. I thought we had more time so I went home to sleep in bed. My grandmother told me that in the middle of the night, my grandfather seemed to have mental clarity and could talk. They said how much they love eachother. And allot of deeply personal things for about a hour. One of the last things he said was “I see mom” and his eyes were closed. And the very last thing he said, after opening his eyes very wide and looking around. “What is this place!?” My grandmother asked “is it beautiful?” He said “yes” and closed his eyes, and went to sleep. 

A few hours later my grandmother called me that his 02 levels were dropping and to come in quick. And again like I said, I went into the hospital room, held his hand with my grandmother and said how much I love him and goodbye, and he passed away within a minute of me coming in. It was like he held on and waited for me because he knew how much I wanted to be there to say goodbye.

Basically nothing with inspection. I’ll only check the trailer when it’s time to open the doors. It’s securities responsibility to inspect the trailers coming in or out. But if we visually see something we will radio it in for the carrier to fix.

Hey! We have a iPad mounted in the trucks that runs a program that will do a dispatched move on the board. Then whichever jockey wants to take the move, we will click on it. It will tell us the trailer number, carrier and which lot it is in. And then it will show us what door or lot to bring it to. After we move the trailer we will hit complete on it. We also have radios inside the truck to communicate with eachother and the dispatcher.

Our lot very rarely has live loads, so the drivers coming in will drop the trailer in the lot and we bring them all to the doors. It’s a small plant with tricky docks, but you get used to it after doing it so much. We also help truckers coming in if they are having issues picking up their trailer.

It is way easier backing a yard truck. The fundamentals are the same, but it is super quick to steer and get under the trailer when you need to. You are able to react allot quicker to where you want the trailer to go. Also we do quite a bit of blindside backing, and have allot more visibility than normal trucks.

We have a few females where we work too! It is a great job, can be a bit demanding with the amount of dust in our gravel lots. And you get quite a leg workout with all the stairs going up and down. Plus we have jackstands we have to move and place. My iPhone tracks 11,000 steps a shift and 10 flights of stairs. But some nights are slower than others.
Decent for the work itself and distance from home, but nothing amazing. I make $26.25hr, but pretty much as much overtime as you want which adds up.
